nameStory: Purple Chinese houses gets its whimsical name from the tiered, pagoda-like arrangement of its flowers, which stack up the stem like the stories of a traditional Chinese building. The purple and white blooms are arranged in whorls around the stem, creating distinct 'floors' that reminded early botanists of multi-story architecture.
description: Purple Chinese houses is a charming annual wildflower native to California that occasionally shows up as a garden escape in New England. This slender plant grows 1-2 feet tall with delicate, snapdragon-like flowers arranged in distinctive tiers up the stem. The two-toned purple and white flowers bloom in spring and early summer, creating an eye-catching display that's hard to miss once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive two-lipped flowers with purple upper petals and white or pale lower petals, arranged in whorls that stack up the stem like floors of a building. Each flower is about half an inch long with a tubular shape.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are oval to lance-shaped, with a soft texture and slightly toothed edges. Upper leaves may be alternate rather than opposite, feeling tender and slightly sticky to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright annual that grows 1-2 feet tall with a somewhat delicate appearance. Stems are square in cross-section and may branch near the top.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. The capsules develop where the flowers were, maintaining the tiered arrangement up the stem.

habitat: In New England, purple Chinese houses is extremely rare and typically found only as a garden escape near cultivated areas or disturbed soils. When it does appear, it prefers sunny to partly shaded locations with well-drained soil, often in gardens, waste areas, or along paths where seeds may have been accidentally introduced.

seasonality.spring: Flowers begin blooming in late spring, with the distinctive purple and white tiered blooms becoming the plant's most noticeable feature. Young plants emerge and grow rapidly during cool, moist spring weather.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming through early summer, with seed capsules beginning to form on lower flower whorls while upper flowers may still be opening. Plants may struggle in hot, dry summer conditions.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse, with the annual plant dying back completely. Look for dried stems with empty seed capsules still showing the characteristic tiered arrangement.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this is an annual plant. Seeds lie dormant in the soil, waiting for spring germination conditions.

funFact: Despite being called 'Chinese houses,' this plant is actually a California native that has never grown wild in China - the name comes purely from the architectural appearance of its stacked flower whorls, which early botanists thought resembled traditional Chinese pagodas!
confusionNotes: The tiered flower arrangement is so distinctive that purple Chinese houses is rarely confused with other plants when in bloom. Out of bloom, it might be mistaken for other members of the plantain family, but the opposite leaves and square stems help distinguish it from most similar species.
contextualKnowledge: Purple Chinese houses belongs to the plantain family (Plantaginaceae), which also includes snapdragons, penstemons, and plantains - quite a diverse group! The genus name Collinsia honors Zaccheus Collins, an early American botanist, while 'heterophylla' means 'different leaves,' referring to how the upper and lower leaves can have different arrangements.
compareHints: Purple Chinese houses differs from its relative small-flowered blue-eyed mary by having much more prominent, colorful flowers arranged in obvious tiers, rather than tiny, inconspicuous blooms. The purple and white color combination is also distinctive, compared to the mostly blue or white flowers of other Collinsia species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Small-flowered blue-eyed mary is much smaller and more delicate than its western relative Purple Chinese Houses, which has showier, larger flowers and grows taller.
